name: Hana Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I began playing handbells for pay after my children left home. I am a junior player in a touring community ensemble, record short parts and teach three beginners, and I still ask the lead player to listen for my timing. I like the moment a group finds one pulse; carrying the bell cases between buses is less charming.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the work and home figures add up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner repairs bicycles, and our grown children live elsewhere. We have a small mortgage and nine months of expenses saved; a long school concert contract pays me well for a junior musician, and there are other venues nearby. I use AI every day for draft routes and booking replies, but I check the actual calls and never put pupil recordings into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensemble that a faster route sheet is useful if the player and rehearsal fees remain clear. My hands and ears still do the bell part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school concerts and three pupils are paid through the term, and my partner’s workshop has regular repairs. Nine months saved lets us meet the mortgage through an ordinary cancellation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the paid concerts, recordings and three pupils, and ask for the next school term’s rehearsal fees in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension statement before discussing retirement, and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our work and money in this picture. I can plan from paid concert dates and a real pension statement, not a birthday alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why request the pension statement now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know the exact amount or date yet. A statement will let my partner and me read the number before we make any promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy lighter bell cases?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if cleared paid concerts cover them after bills and the reserve stays intact. The old cases are awkward but safe.

I would keep **live handbell playing** in the school concerts.
think: I need an **actual pension statement** before naming any retirement date or claiming a payment amount.
do: Keep **concerts, recordings and pupils** with written next-term fees.
Request **pension statement** before retirement decisions and save fifth of cleared extra recording fees after bills toward twelve months.
feel: I feel **calm** about paid work and household bills.
S0.quote: I can plan from paid concert dates and a real pension statement, not a birthday alone.
fieldNote: Her **school concert contract** and nine-month reserve make the plateau secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the ensemble to show us which recording and booking hours are still paid. I would also tell families that a handbell class needs sound instruments and an experienced paid helper supervising my first-steps teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect fewer short recording calls and perhaps a smaller school contract as planning becomes cheap. That would cut my own fees, even with nine months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid concerts and pupils and ask for written renewal rates. If two monthly recording calls disappear, I would offer a separate Saturday handbell class only after the hall gives me a written room booking and eight families pay deposits covering my basic teaching and preparation, an experienced paid helper supervising my first-steps teaching, bell hire and travel; I would inspect every bell and replace an unsafe one or defer and refund the whole class if eight safe paid places cannot remain, and renew in the first year only if eight paid places still cover every wage and cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real slice of music pay shrinking. The reserve gives me room to test a class, not a reason to ask anyone to work free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspect the bells before class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cracked handle can hurt a child. If I cannot replace that bell safely, I will defer and refund the whole class unless a safe replacement restores eight paid places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the helper volunteer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the helper’s setup and class hours are part of the eight-place price. My preparation time is in that price too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensemble that 2028 thinking AGI could handle booking and make a recording before a robot rings bells around 2031. I would ask for the paid school dates on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short recording fees to stop and the school concert contract to lose a few paid dates in 2028. Nine months saved helps, but losing both would lower what I bring home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed school dates and keep three pupils. In the first year after 2028, if recording calls end and school dates shrink, I would apply for a posted paid school music-room assistant role only if my secondary schooling and experience qualify, its written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport works; I would keep playing and teaching until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing pay quickly, though the reserve and several nearby venues give me some time. A school job still needs an actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a school accept your training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know until I read a posting. My secondary schooling and ensemble experience must meet that school’s stated requirements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop the new class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I have no written room and eight paid places covering my work, helper and safe bells, yes. A class promise cannot replace a signed wage.

I would ask for **paid school dates** on paper.
think: I expect **recording and concert fees** to fall.
A **nine-month reserve** buys some time to search, not replacement income for lost school dates.
do: Keep **school concerts and pupils** with signed dates before 2028 and until a signed replacement offer.
Seek **posted school assistant role** after 2028 recording/date losses; require qualifying schooling/experience, written replacement net after travel and workable transport.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fast cuts to my own fees.
S2.quote: A school job still needs an actual vacancy.
fieldNote: The **2028 risk** reaches booking and recordings before capable robot bell playing.
A **school move** requires a posted paid role, qualifying education and written net income replacing losses.

steps.text: Keep paid school concerts and three pupils until signed replacement offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell families that five years is time to make fair class agreements. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot bell players around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording calls may fade before live school concerts do. I could test a small class with paying families, but I need a room and safe bells before I take their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep school concerts and pupils and secure a written Saturday room booking before taking deposits. If two monthly recording calls disappear, I would open a separate bell class only with eight deposits covering my basic teaching and preparation, an experienced paid helper supervising my first-steps teaching, bell hire and travel, after inspecting the bells; I would replace any unsafe bell or defer and refund the whole class if eight safe paid places cannot remain, and in the first year after 2031 renew only when eight paid places cover the same wages and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording pay over the next few years. Five years gives me time to check a room and real enrolment, not to count a waiting list as cash. A waiting list for my Saturday handbell class is not cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if seven families pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not book the helper or run the class at a loss. I would return the deposits or wait for another date with eight paid places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use an AI lesson recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload a child’s voice without written family permission. I already use AI for routes, but any class audio would be checked by my own ears and kept private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot bell players around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask who gets the rehearsal fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might play fewer concerts, but I have no retirement date until I read the pension statement. Nine months saved and the school contract keep the next few years steady, not every future term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep school concerts and pupils, request my actual pension statement and save a fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months. Over the decade I would run a separate bell class only after a written room booking and eight deposits cover my basic teaching/preparation, paid helper, hire and travel, replacing unsafe bells or deferring and refunding the whole class below eight safe paid places; in the first year after 2036 I would renew only on the same paid and safe terms and keep school work while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording work. Current school fees and our reserve hold the next few years, but I want facts before changing my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise to retire at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would read the pension statement with my partner and compare it with our bills. An unchecked pension figure cannot be my retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the room is available only by word of mouth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for the written booking before collecting deposits. The helper and families need a definite room and date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recordings and school dates could shrink before I find another paid role. Signed school dates, a real qualifying vacancy and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a child’s bell before the first note. A paid handbell class place is not a safe place until the instrument works.

headlineQuote: A paid handbell class place is not a safe place until the instrument works.
portrait: Hana is a **junior handbell player** still learning, with secondary schooling and unusually strong concert fees.
She has **nine months saved**, a bicycle-repairing partner, grown children and a small mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** for routes and replies, while keeping pupil audio private.
She tests **separate paid classes** only with written room, full wages, safe bells and real deposits.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut recordings and school dates before a replacement role appears.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **signed school dates**, a qualifying vacancy and written replacement net after travel.
